name: Friendship Bench: problem-solving therapy by lay health workers in Zimbabwe
summary: Friendship Bench trains lay health workers (mostly older women, 'grandmothers') to give problem-solving talk therapy on benches at clinics across Zimbabwe; it saw about 296,000 clients in 2024. We estimate roughly 117 WELLBYs per $1,000 donated, around 16 times GiveDirectly, with a very wide range (under 1× to over 200× even with the shared exchange rates at their defaults). The biggest uncertainties are what Friendship Bench actually spends (it publishes no audited accounts), which of two very different trials of the program reflects routine delivery, how much of the effect survives when about half of clients get a single session instead of six, and how long the effect lasts.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What Friendship Bench's bench program in Zimbabwe cost in 2024, including its share of management and fundraising. Friendship Bench Zimbabwe doesn't publish audited accounts, so total spending is a judgment bracketed by its US affiliate's Form 990, its own budget and its own cost-per-client figure.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Clients seen in 2024, as Friendship Bench reports them. Not independently verified.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What a full course of Friendship Bench therapy does for one client, in standard deviations of depression and distress scales, blending the two Friendship Bench trials with meta-analyses of psychotherapy in low- and middle-income countries, then how long it lasts and what that is in WELLBYs.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with the government health system, and clients getting fewer sessions than in the trials. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: WELLBYs for clients and their households, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With salary sacrifice counted, your dollar is credited with its share only.

rows.label: Friendship Bench Zimbabwe total spending, 2024
rows.explainer:
Friendship Bench Zimbabwe publishes no financial statements (its 2025 annual report names Vista Chartered Accountants as auditor, but the accounts aren't online), so this is bracketed from three of its own documents:

- **Low, $3.1M**: the 2024 Form 990 of its US fundraising arm, Friendship Bench Inc, shows total expenses of $3,103,651 and no salaries, so it is mostly grants out. We couldn't see the grant schedule (ProPublica's filing download is behind a bot check), and some may have gone to US work (Friendship Bench DC), so this is an indicator rather than a strict floor. Friendship Bench Zimbabwe also had direct funding (USAID until early 2025, WHO, research grants), which pushes the other way.
- **Best, $4.0M**: its 2024 and 2023 annual reports ask for "US$8 million" over January 2024–December 2025, about $4M a year; $4.0M ÷ 295,770 clients is $13.5 per client, the low end of the charity's own "$13–16.50 per client".
- **High, $4.9M**: $16.50 per client × 295,770 clients.

A budget is a fundraising ask, not spending; if the audited accounts become available they replace this row.

rows.label: Program share of total spending

source.title: Friendship Bench Annual Report 2024
source.page: p. 20, 'Partner with us on this journey'
source.quote: we need to raise US$8 million: $4.9M (60%) to [programme] ... $3.1M (40%) to Marketing, finance, HR, administration, fundraising costs

rows.explainer: The budget split between programme activities (grandmothers, health-worker training, peer groups, youth buddies, the online Open Line, research) and support costs. 40% support is high for a delivery charity; the range allows for actual spending tilting either way. With the overhead ratio below, this share cancels out of the cost (cost = total × bench share) and only matters for how the cost is presented.

rows.label: Program expenses (all programs)
rows.explainer: Total spending times the programme share in Friendship Bench's own budget.

rows.label: Share of program spending on the Zimbabwe bench program
rows.explainer: The modelled program is therapy on the bench in Zimbabwe (face to face and on the online Open Line) plus the Circle Kubatana Tose peer groups clients join afterwards, since the trials tested that package. Not modelled: research (much of it funded by separate grants), Friendship Bench in a Box training for partners abroad, and the community hub. Their budget lines aren't split out; 85% assumes they take about a sixth of programme spending, with 70% and 95% as the ends. A lower share makes the bench program cheaper per client.

rows.label: Spending on the bench program, 2024 (before overhead)
rows.explainer: Programme expenses times the bench program's share.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Cost of the bench program, including overhead
rows.explainer: Friendship Bench's own spending only. The time of government village health workers and clinic nurses, and the clinics themselves, aren't in it; they lower the attribution share instead.

rows.label: Clients seen by implementing partners, 2024

source.title: Friendship Bench Annual Report 2024
source.page: p. 9, province table, 'Partner-ships' column, row '# of Clients seen'

rows.explainer: Clients seen by other organisations that Friendship Bench trained ("implementing partners"). Their delivery costs are theirs, not in Friendship Bench's spending, so we leave these clients out rather than pay for them with Friendship Bench's cost.

rows.label: Unique clients per reported client
rows.explainer: The count is Friendship Bench's own administrative figure, not independently verified, and the reports don't say whether a client who returns in a new episode, or moves between benches, is counted twice. Its monitoring samples are drawn from these registers: in 2023 the team "managed to call" 12,373 of 17,463 sampled clients and 3,326 completed the six-week survey (annual report 2023, client-care table). Low completion fits real but hard-to-reach clients, but doesn't prove every register entry is a distinct person. 95% allows for some double counting; 85% for more; 100% if the count is exact.

rows.label: Clients seen in 2024 (Friendship Bench's own delivery)
rows.explainer: Reported clients, less those seen by implementing partners, times the share that are unique people: about 274,000.

rows.label: Clients seen in 2024, as reported

source.title: Friendship Bench Annual Report 2024
source.quote: 295770 TOTAL NUMBER OF CLIENTS SEEN BY FRIENDSHIP BENCH IN 2024

rows.explainer: All clients who started therapy in 2024: 285,900 face to face with the grandmothers and partners, 9,870 on the WhatsApp Open Line. It counts everyone who started, so partial attendance is handled in the delivery adjustment. Clients are screened with the Shona Symptom Questionnaire (SSQ-14); in Friendship Bench's 2025 follow-up cohort 2,990 of 3,009 clients with scores were above the cut-off at baseline, so nearly all clients have symptoms. The count is the charity's own administrative figure, not independently verified. Reach was 220,766 in 2023 and 336,215 in 2025; 2024 is used because it is the year we have spending figures for.

rows.label: Cost per client
rows.explainer: About $12.40 per client Friendship Bench itself saw. Checks: Friendship Bench quotes "$13–16.50 per client" (KBF Africa Prize page), which covers all its activities; its 2026 budget asks for $4.1M to serve 380,000 people ($10.80); a 2022 economic analysis of the 2020 program implies roughly $14–17 per patient in 2019 dollars.

rows.label: Effect in the Harare trial (Chibanda 2016), SD
rows.explainer: Our standardisation of the trial's primary outcome. At 6 months the SSQ-14 mean was 3.81 (95% CI 3.28–4.34) with the Friendship Bench and 8.90 (8.33–9.47) with enhanced usual care, among 521 people followed up. Backing the standard deviations out of those intervals gives about 4.4 and 4.7, so the 4.86-point difference is about 1.08 SD. The PHQ-9 depression score gives a similar picture (mean difference −6.36; PHQ-9 ≥11 in 13.7% vs 49.9%). The range allows for the intervals being cluster-adjusted (which would make the true SD smaller and the effect bigger) and for sampling error. Participants received a median of 5 of 6 sessions.

rows.label: Effect in the rural Bikita trial (Haas 2023), SD

source.title: Haas et al. 2023, JAMA Network Open: Friendship Bench and ART outcomes in rural Zimbabwe
source.quote: The intervention improved CMD symptoms, but the effect was smaller than previously shown in an urban setting.

rows.explainer: Our standardisation. In 516 adults on HIV treatment, delivered by village health workers (88% completed all six sessions), the SSQ-14 fell 1.65, 1.56 and 1.63 points more than with standard care at 3, 6 and 9 months (adjusted, Table 2), but PHQ-9 depression scores barely differed (adjusted −0.49, −0.14, −0.19, all with intervals spanning zero). The paper gives no follow-up SDs; using the Harare trial's (about 4.5), the SSQ-14 effect is about 0.36 SD and the PHQ-9 effect about 0, so 0.2 is their average. The low end takes the null depression result at face value; the high end takes the SSQ-14. The control arm improved a lot, which the authors put down to enhanced standard care.

rows.label: Weight on the urban Harare trial (versus rural Bikita)
rows.explainer: The two trials are about the same size (573 and 516 people) but differ in how much they resemble the program as it runs today. In 2024 about a fifth of Friendship Bench's own clients were in Harare and Bulawayo (annual report 2024, p. 9: 40,684 and 18,278 of 288,388); the rest are seen in smaller towns and rural districts by village and community health workers supervised by clinic nurses, as in the Bikita trial. Against that, the Bikita sample (people on HIV treatment, milder depression at baseline) may have had less room to improve, and its control arm got enhanced care. 20% weights the trials by the delivery mix; 50% treats them as equally informative; 35% is between.

rows.label: Friendship Bench trials, weighted effect (SD)
rows.explainer: Weighted average of the two Friendship Bench trials, about 0.51 SD. They disagree a lot: the urban trial is one of the largest effects in the literature, the rural one near the bottom.

rows.label: Psychotherapy for depression in low- and middle-income settings, bias-adjusted (SD)

source.title: Tong, Miguel, Panagiotopoulou, Karyotaki, Cuijpers 2023, Psychological Medicine 53(16):7473
source.page: Results: publication bias and risk-of-bias sensitivity analyses

rows.explainer: What a typical psychotherapy for depression achieves in non-Western, mostly low- and middle-income settings. The raw pooled effect is g = 1.10, but small, biased trials inflate it: the selection-model correction gives 0.49 (trim-and-fill 0.60, limit meta-analysis 0.42), and the low-risk-of-bias trials give 0.69 (our high end). The low end, 0.32, is the individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 11 task-shared (lay-delivered) trials in LMICs (Karyotaki et al. 2022, JAMA Psychiatry), the closest reference class to the Friendship Bench. All are measured soon after treatment (about 3–4 months).

rows.label: Weight on the Friendship Bench trials versus the meta-analytic prior
rows.explainer: Two trials of this exact program against a prior from over a hundred trials of similar ones. Charity-specific trials are more relevant, but two trials that disagree this much (1.08 vs 0.2) carry a lot of noise, and the larger one was run by the program's founder in its home setting. Half and half is our best guess; 25% leans on the literature, 75% on the program's own trials. Neither end discounts publication bias again: the prior is already corrected and the two trials are all the Friendship Bench trials there are.

rows.label: Effect at the end of a full course (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: The weighted blend: about 0.50 SD on depression and distress scales for someone who gets the full six-session course, as in the trials. Under half of the Harare trial's effect (0.46× of 1.08).

rows.label: Years until the effect has faded
rows.explainer:
An input rather than initial effect ÷ decay, so the effect size doesn't enter twice. The model assumes the effect falls in a straight line to zero.

Anchors: in the largest meta-analysis of long-term effects (Cuijpers et al. 2026, World Psychiatry, 191 trials, mostly high-income; Table 2), the effect is 0.544 SD at 3 months, 0.434 at 6 months, 0.389 at one year, and then flat: 0.390 at two years, 0.392 at three, 0.397 at five, though the authors warn that data beyond two years are sparse. In the rural Friendship Bench trial the SSQ-14 difference didn't shrink between 3 and 9 months. A straight line through the meta-analysis' 71% of peak at two years would imply about 7 years.

We use 5 years (80% of the effect left at one year, 60% at two) because the plateau rests on few, attrition-prone long follow-ups, nearly all from high-income countries, where relapse after stressful life events in poor households is likely less common. 2 years is the low end (relapse-heavy setting, plateau an artefact of who stays in follow-ups); 8 years takes the plateau at face value. The trials measured the effect at 6–9 months, but the line starts at the end of treatment, which errs slightly on the low side.

rows.label: Decay of the effect (SDs per year)
rows.explainer: Context: the implied linear decay, about 0.10 SD a year.

rows.label: Total effect per person (SD-years)
rows.explainer: Area of the triangle: linear decay from the initial effect to zero.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person given a full course
rows.explainer: SD-years converted to life-satisfaction points with the shared factor (2 WELLBYs per SD-year).

rows.label: Household size
rows.explainer: The shared figure for psychotherapy recipients in Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe, which includes this program's setting, so no country-specific replacement is needed.

rows.label: Household multiplier (recipient plus spillovers)
rows.explainer: Each other household member is credited with the shared spillover share of the client's own gain (16%, range 5–30%). This adds about 60% to the total, and is the least studied part of the chain.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer:
**Anchor.** In Tong et al. 2023 (the source of our prior), trials at low risk of bias, which includes blinded or less biased outcome measurement, show g = 0.69 against 1.10 for all trials: a ratio of about 0.63. Half of our blended effect comes from the meta-analytic prior, which is already corrected for publication bias, and that correction captures part of this gap. The other half comes from the two Friendship Bench trials, which aren't corrected. Applying a 0.63-type discount to the trial half only gives 0.5 × 0.63 + 0.5 × 1 ≈ 0.8. Three refinements roughly cancel: the Harare trial had masked outcome assessors (one of Tong's low-risk criteria), which argues for less discount; the Bikita trial was unblinded; and the prior pools waitlist-controlled trials, which overstate effects against usual care (Friendship Bench's comparator), which argues for more. The low end, 0.6, applies the full risk-of-bias gap to everything (treating the publication-bias correction as a different problem); the high end, 1, assumes both trials and the corrected prior are unbiased.

What the discount stands for, i.e. what the blended effect doesn't already account for:

- **Self-report and demand effects**: both trials measure symptoms by interview with the same questionnaires clients see in therapy, and the comparison arms knew they weren't treated. Social-desirability bias in symptom scales is a known problem for psychotherapy trials in low-income settings.
- **Routine delivery versus trials**: at national scale, over 2,000 lay workers are supervised by Friendship Bench and health-ministry staff, not research teams; clients' own feedback in 2025 names "missed counselling sessions and incomplete follow-ups" as the main complaint, and the 2025 USAID withdrawal strained supervision. Session counts are handled separately (delivery adjustment); this covers the quality of each session.

Not adjusted for here: publication bias (the prior is already corrected) and the gap between the urban and rural trials (it is in the blend). Friendship Bench's own monitoring (85% of followed-up clients "recovered" at six weeks in 2025) has no control group and reached only 22% of the cohort, so it isn't used to raise this.

The scale-up dilution has no good reference class: the closest is the rural trial, already in the blend, whose effect was a fifth of the urban one.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The trial effects are already relative to (enhanced) usual care, which covers natural recovery and the little help clients get otherwise. What remains: whether some clients would have found other talk therapy without Friendship Bench. Zimbabwe has very few mental-health workers (the 2025 annual report cites a 75–85% treatment gap in under-resourced settings), and Friendship Bench is the main community provider, so most would not. 0.85 allows for church, NGO and clinic counselling filling some of the gap, 1 for none.

rows.label: Friendship Bench's share of credit (shared with the health ministry)
rows.explainer: The therapy is delivered at government clinics by community and village health workers who belong to the Ministry of Health and Child Care's system (in the rural trial they were "selected from the existing pool of village health workers" and supervised by clinic nurses), and the program is being handed over to the ministry, with full integration planned by 2028. Their time and the clinics aren't in our cost, so Friendship Bench gets the share of credit it would have as a share of the total cost: 80% if the government's in-kind contribution is about a quarter of Friendship Bench's own spending. Lay workers get only small allowances (in a rural Friendship Bench rollout in Zaka district they worked "on a primarily voluntary basis" for USD 10 a month for transport and airtime: Kidia et al. 2024, Social Science & Medicine, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11221631), which is why the share is high; 60% if nurse supervision and clinic time are larger than we think, 100% if they're negligible.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: With full credit for shared outcomes switched on, the charity gets the whole outcome.

rows.label: Share of clients who attend only one session
rows.explainer:
Friendship Bench's researchers write that in routine care "most recipients received between one and three sessions" and that "up to 48% of the participants only complete one (1) therapy session" (Shava et al. 2026, single-session therapy protocol, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13295822/, introduction and sample-size section; no data source given).

Its own administrative counts are inconsistent. The quarterly impact reports record about one follow-up session per client seen (Q2 2024: 71,388 clients, 75,256 follow-up sessions; Q1 2025: 79,172 clients, 82,245 follow-up sessions), which fits about half of clients stopping after one session and the rest averaging about three. But the annual reports record far fewer (2024: 47,073 follow-ups for 295,770 clients; 2025: 3,284 for 336,215), as does the Q2 2026 report (2,726 for 86,832). The quarterlies can't be reconciled with the annual totals, so the annual rows look truncated or defined differently, and the recent drop may also reflect real cuts after USAID funding ended in 2025.

We use 50%, matching the researchers' figure and the 2024–25 quarterlies. 35% if more clients return than the researchers say; 80% if the low annual counts are the true ones. Asking Friendship Bench what a "follow-up session" is would settle it.

rows.label: Effect of a single session, relative to a full course
rows.explainer: Single-session interventions do have effects: a meta-analysis of 50 trials in young people found g = 0.32 (Schleider and Weisz 2017), against about 0.5–0.6 for full courses of psychotherapy, and a review co-authored by Friendship Bench's founder found five of six small adult trials positive for depression (Kim, Ryu and Chibanda 2023, BMC Psychology). For depression specifically, the same meta-analysis is reported to have found 0.18 for single sessions against 0.28 for standard youth depression programs, a ratio of about 0.64 (from secondary coverage; the paper was not accessible). So one session gets about half the effect of a full course, if anything conservatively; 30% if single sessions in this setting are mostly a first visit that doesn't get to problem-solving, 70% if they are as good as the best single-session evidence suggests. This is where the dose-response evidence the skill asks for comes from: it is weak.

rows.label: Effect for clients with two or more sessions, relative to a full course
rows.explainer: Clients who come back mostly get two or three sessions (the researchers' "between one and three"; the 2024 administrative count implies about two on average), against a median of five (Harare) or six (Bikita) in the trials. 75% assumes the first sessions carry most of the benefit, as is common in psychotherapy; 55% if the effect builds steadily with sessions, 95% if two or three are nearly enough.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (sessions received versus the trials)
rows.explainer: The share of a full course's effect the average client gets, given how many sessions clients actually attend: about 0.63. Session quality is in the evidence adjustment, not here.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, about 0.38. Combined with the blend, the effect credited per client is about 18% of the Harare trial's effect (0.46 × 0.38), before duration and spillovers.

rows.label: WELLBYs
WELLBYs per dollar
Staff pay as a share of total cost
rows.explainer: No functional expense statement is published. Friendship Bench is a people business: supervisors, trainers, data and customer-care staff, research and head-office staff, plus allowances to lay workers. 45% is typical of labour-intensive health delivery NGOs; 30–60% as the range. It only matters with salary sacrifice switched on, and then only a little.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs
rows.explainer: Below the repo's 15% for large delivery charities: in Zimbabwe, internationally funded NGO jobs usually pay as well as or better than local alternatives, so most staff give up little. The lay health workers do give their time for small allowances, which pushes the gap up; 0 to 25% covers both readings.
